analytic.title: A Scheduler Support Unit for Reactive Microprocessors

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Efficient scheduling mechanisms are essential for implementing real-time operating systems on embedded microprocessors. Reactive processors provide mechanisms and an instruction set architecture more suitable for dealing with external signals than it is the case with traditional interrupts. By extending the reactive framework further we demonstrate simple and efficient hardwareimplemented scheduling of tasks with static priorities. The scheduler support unit is added to the reactive microprocessor core. The real-time scheduler shows substantial improvement of performance over the conventional approach of using prioritized interrupts.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The efficiency of a real-time scheduler can be determined by how much it elongates the response time of a task due to the overhead resulting from preemption, priority resolution and context switching. Hard real-time systems require that all tasks have response times which are less than their corresponding deadlines. We are interested in increasing the efficiency of a scheduler by accelerating the underlying scheduling mechanisms as well as improving its predictability by exploiting parallelisms by direct hardware support.

Modern embedded microprocessors support scheduling via interrupts, which usually combine preemption, priority resolution and context switching in an inseparable mechanism with associated latency due to their inherent sequential nature.

In this paper, we introduce direct hardware support for scheduling that improves efficiency and predictability of real-time schedulers and demonstrate it on the example of reactive processors [1]. The mechanism extends into a simple programming model supported by a small set of dedicated instructions. This enables a very simple and safe method of coding real-time schedulers. The scheduler support is isolated into a hardware functional unit called scheduler support unit (SSU). The SSU is prototyped and added to the reactive microprocessor. Performance evaluation of the proposed approach reveals significant improvement over interrupt based real-time schedulers.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: The Multiple Active Context System (MACS) architecture, which executes a program with high predictability, is presented in [2]. It tracks multiple task contexts in hardware and performs static pipelined scheduling. It is designed to absorb unpredictable latencies of memory access and pipeline stalls in an effort to provide a predictable and high performance real-time processor. The SSU approach, unlike MACS, is loosely coupled with the host processor's datapath that makes it applicable to almost any processor. The concept of tracking multiple task contexts in hardware is common to our approach and MACS. However, unlike MCAS, we provide the instruction set architecture (ISA) support for scheduling.

Real-time scheduling on a Simultaneous Multithreading (SMT) processor is explored in [3]. SMT processors provide direct support for general purpose operating systems via dynamic pipeline scheduling to exploit both instruction-level and thread-level parallelism [4,5]. Due to the inherently speculative nature of dynamic pipeline scheduling the approach is not suitable for hard real-time scheduling.

A memory-mapped on-chip peripheral module called the Real-Time Task Manager (RTM) presented in [6] carries out task scheduling, event management and time tracking. However, the SSU in our approach is controlled directly by dedicated instructions and the scheduling itself is performed within the SSU.

The approach presented here for the SSU design is an extension of the work on reactive processors [1], which incorporate explicit instructions for preemption and priority resolution of based on the signals that interconnect the processor with external environment. However, the original reactive processors did not support execution of multiple tasks and real-time scheduling due to the lack of two key features: (1) no queuing of two or more simultaneously released tasks for later execution and (2) inability to automatically save and restore task contexts. The approach presented in this paper has taken the concept of a reactive processor to the practical domain of embedded real-time systems.

div.head: Architectural Framework
div.p: A real-time system consists of a set of (reactive) tasks that can interact with the external environment and between themselves thorough the signals and operations that can be performed on those signals (emit, check for presence, wait for signal presence and preempt) [7]. The tasks state is controlled by the scheduler through state the transitions as illustrated in Figure 1 and supported by the SSU. All tasks are initially in the Inactive state and remain there until released by external signals. Once a task has been released, it enters the Active state and becomes ready to be executed. When a task is given access to the processor, it enters the Executing state. Subsequently, when a task completes its execution, it returns to the Inactive state. A task that is currently executing may be preempted whenever a higher priority task is released. Whenever a new task is released, the scheduler must resolve the priorities of all active tasks along with the currently executing task to select the highest priority task for execution. Similarly, when a task completes execution, the scheduler must again resolve the priorities of all active tasks and select the highest priority task for execution.

Some practical constraints are further introduced. It is assumed that real-time tasks are periodic and independent from each other, and their priorities are statically assigned, making the SSU applicable to the schedulers with the Deadline Monotonic (DM) and the Rate Monotonic (RM) scheduling policy. The events that release tasks arrive into the system asynchronously and are queued for execution at a later point in time.

div.head: Task Abstraction and Implementation
div.p: The Task is considered an object that consists of two parts: a Task Descriptor, which is used by the scheduler, and the Task Code, which implements the task functionality. The Task Descriptor consists of three elements: Task State Indicator, TSI, (Active or Inactive), Task Release Signal, TSR, (identifier of the signal line that triggers release of the task), and Task Context, TC, (minimal information necessary to start or resume execution of the task). A forth implicit element is the statically assigned task priority, which is given by the descriptor index in the task-table, as depicted in Figure 2. The task-table, maintained by the scheduler (SSU), has to be initialized before scheduling is enabled. In addition, the last task (Task N) is the background task that runs whenever the system is reset, powered up or all the schedulable tasks are completed and are in Inactive state waiting to be released. The Executing Task Index points to the Task Descriptor of the currently executing task and it is used in the task context switching process. The TSI and TRS fields are accessed by the SSU logic to enable updating of task states and to resolve priorities once a new task is released or the current task is completed.

div.head: Hardware/Software Interaction
div.p: The SSU hardware is responsible for monitoring of the task release input signal lines. Each newly released task has its state information updated to Active and is queued along with other active tasks, where the queue is represented with all entries in the task table which have state indicator set to Active. Then the priorities of all active tasks are resolved in order to select the highest priority task for execution. Notice that the currently executing task is also included during the priority resolution phase. While the hardware is busy carrying out these duties, the processor can continue executing the current task and need not be involved in the scheduling process. If the newly released task is resolved to have higher priority than the currently executing task and the other active tasks, then the processor is preempted and is instructed to switch to the new task's context. Hence, the processor is only stalled by the SSU during context switching. If the newly released task has a lower priority than the currently executing task, the processor continues executing the current task without interruption.

div.head: Scheduling Support Instructions
div.p: The SSU has a number of standalone commands (shown in Table 1) through which it can be controlled. They are aimed at initialization of the task table before scheduling begins, enabling, stopping and resuming scheduling and specification of the context in which a task will be reactivated or resumed after completion of its operation or suspension for some reason, respectively. In our case these commands have been integrated into the reactive processor instruction set and as such exist in the processor assembly language.

div.head: Programming Model for Multitasking
div.p: The concept of SSU allows for a very simple programming model for real-time scheduler and multi- tasking systems. The task code for each task is stored at arbitrary locations in memory. Each task code requires just a single instruction at its end, called SuspendTask, which indicates with which context the task will start after its next release or resumption of operation. Task execution and scheduling is otherwise fully controlled by the SSU. The only additional piece of code that has to be written is the initialization code which initializes the task table before the real-time scheduler starts.

div.head: Table 1 SSU control commands
div.p: The programmer view of the multi-tasking system is illustrated in Figure 3. The initialization code enters task descriptors into the task table. The order of task initialization instructions specifies the task priorities.

Once the system initialization is completed, the scheduling function is enabled and the control is transferred to the background task, which is the only task that is given full control of the SSU (to stop and/or resume scheduling). Once the scheduling of real-time tasks begins (triggered by the occurrence of task release signals), the SSU takes control over the scheduling process. Only when all tasks have completed and there are no active tasks in the system, the control is transferred again to the background task.

div.head: SSU Implementation
div.p: The whole concept of the scheduling framework and estimation of additional resource requirements has been verified on the reactive (open source) microprocessor core, ReMIC [1,7]. For the task context, minimal information, which contains current processor program counter (PC), stack pointer (SP) and condition code (CC) register, is used. The placement of the SSU within the processor is illustrated in Figure 4.

In order to save or restore a task context in a single cycle, a wide datapath, which enables transfer of register contents that represent the task context (PC, SP, CC), is provided between the SSU and the rest of ReMIC datapath. Storage for the task descriptor is split into two parts: TSI and TRS are implemented using flip-flops in the FPGA, while TC is implemented in SRAM memory block.

div.head: Figure 4: Reactive processor with SSU
div.p: The SSU datapath implements the task-table and ETI register and priority resolution circuitry. The SSU control unit handles scheduling and also cooperates with the host processor control unit when an actual context switch occurs. In that case the SSU control unit stalls the processor, enables the actual context to be loaded and guarantees consistency of the processor pipeline. It also executes commands received from the processor. The SSU control unit is implemented as a finite state machine (FSM), shown in Figure 5.

The fact that context switching must take place requires a minor modification of the original processor datapath and control unit. Restoration or change of processor context is the sole decision of the scheduler and is controlled by the context_switch internal signal, which is generated by the SSU control unit FSM.

The entire modified reactive microprocessor, ReMIC, was subsequently synthesized in Altera Stratix EP1S40 FPGA device. Table 2 provides a summary of the synthesis results in logic elements (LE) with the SSU supporting different number of tasks. In order to make comparison of the SSU supported scheduler with a traditional approach which is using priority interrupt scheme to release real-time tasks, we modified the original ReMIC core by adding a priority interrupt mechanism. The resulting processor required typically about 2-3% less LEs for implementation than the one with the SSU. However, it also required quite substantial modification of the original control unit and introduction of a number of new states into its control unit FSM. The performance comparisons are given in the following section.

div.head: Scheduler Performance Analysis
div.p: In order to quantify the improvements gained when using the proposed approach for implementing real-time schedulers, comparison with an hardware prioritized interrupt based scheduling mechanism on the same processor was performed. The first result was that the overhead required for priority resolution and context switching was in average two times larger in interrupt based scheme.

In addition, analyses and comparison of different schedulers on a large number of randomly generated synthetic task-sets were carried out. These task-sets conformed to independently chosen task parameters and were fully schedulable in an ideal zero overhead system, under the Rate-Monotonic scheduling policy. All tasks in any given set were independent from each other. Exact schedulability analysis, using the Response Time Analysis (RTA) method [8], was performed on these synthetic task-sets, which incorporated the overhead associated with the two schedulers. Then, the percentage of task-sets that became un-schedulable under each of the two schedulers with respect to various independent parameters of the task-sets was observed. This enabled characterization of the performance of the proposed approach with respect to a wide variety of possible scheduling scenarios.

For a fair comparison of the two scheduling mechanisms, it was necessary to evaluate their efficiency with respect to four independent parameters: processor utilization factor U, number of tasks per set N, lower bound of task periods T low and upper bound of task periods T delta . As the number of tasks in the set increases, the number of preemptions is expected to increase, forcing high-overhead schedulers to behave poorly. Since the scheduler overhead per task is constant, those sets with increasingly shorter and more frequent tasks are more likely to become un-schedulable. As the variation among the tasks' periods and deadlines decreases, even small delays introduced by the scheduler overhead can cause deadline misses. Finally, as the utilization factor increases, it amplifies the effects noted above. Thus, an efficient scheduling mechanism would keep many of the ideally schedulable tasks still schedulable under heavy processor utilization.

To avoid biasing effects, the task-sets were generated according to the method proposed by Bini et al. [9]. For any given task-set, each of the N tasks has a period within the range [T low , T low × T delta ). Hence, the upper bound was always set as a multiple of the lower bound in order to achieve a wide coverage. Three different benchmark experiments were carried out and in each of them, two of the four parameters were varied while keeping the other two constant. For any given set of these four parameters, 10×10 3 corresponding task-sets were generated and benchmarking analysis for both schedulers performed. Figure 6 illustrates one of the experiments where the first set of benchmark results where the processor utilization factor U and the number of tasks N (N=8 in Figure ) per set were varied. We kept the lower and upper bounds of task periods constant at 1×10 3 and 100×10 3 clock cycles respectively. It is evident from figure that the proposed approach is more efficient than the interrupt based mechanisms in terms of the percentage of task-sets that can be scheduled when the processor utilization factor is high. Figure 7 shows the overall characterization of the performance of SSU based approach when varying the processor utilization factor and the size of each taskset. In the ideal case, the surface in figure would be a flat plane since all task-sets that we generated were initially fully schedulable. Similar analysis has been performed for interrupt based approach and the SSU approach was in average 14% more efficient than hardware prioritized interrupts.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: A generic hardware support for real-time schedulers for reactive microprocessors has been developed. The scheduler support unit monitors input signal lines for task release, keeps track of task states and makes scheduling decisions based on priorities of released tasks. The programming model utilizes the underlying hardware support via dedicated new instructions providing flexibility and scalability to the implementation of realtime schedulers.
The SSU concept has been verified on ReMIC reactive microprocessor implemented on FPGA device and requires between 6.1% (for two tasks) and 15.7% (for 16 tasks) additional hardware resources.
The SSU based scheduler was compared to one based on the interrupts. Consistent performance improvement for a variety of task-sets was obtained for the SSU based approach.
The proposed framework is currently applicable only to static priority scheduling policies; however, with relatively simple extensions it can accommodate dynamic priority real-time scheduling.
